entries.title: Answer a research question with a graded, cited evidence set rather than an impression. Retrieval, verification, gap analysis and synthesis run as a loop that stops on a stated saturation condition, and every claim leaves the loop carrying its type, evidence level, confidence and the source that was actually reached.
entries.summary: A question arrives whose answer will drive an engineering, architectural or adoption decision, where the cost of being confidently wrong exceeds the cost of researching it properly — technology selection, vendor or library evaluation, state-of-practice questions, regulatory or protocol questions, and any question where sources are known or likely to conflict. | stages: Scope the question → Retrieve for primary sources → Verify identity, date and standing → Extract graded claims → Seek independent corroboration → Resolve conflicts by precedence → Self-critique the evidence set → Stop on saturation, not on exhaustion → Synthesise and report

entries.summary: Latency, throughput or page-load complaints backed by a symptom; a measured regression with a known approximate date; capacity planning for a known event; before scaling infrastructure; when setting budgets for a new product or redesign. | stages: Agree the budget and the population → Capture the baseline → Profile and attribute → Rank and select → Fix in remove-first order → Verify with the same method → Confirm in the field → Enforce the budget

entries.title: Take a change from merged to production and settled — version and changelog discipline, reproducible build, progressive rollout with health gates, instant rollback rehearsed, observation against leading indicators, and cleanup of flags and shims afterwards.

entries.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
entries.summary: Shows that prompting with a few worked examples containing intermediate reasoning steps ('chain of thought') substantially improves complex reasoning in sufficiently large language models. Reports state-of-the-art GSM8K accuracy for a 540B-parameter model prompted with eight exemplars, surpassing fine-tuned GPT-3 with a verifier.

entries.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
entries.summary: Generalises chain-of-thought from a single left-to-right chain to a tree of intermediate 'thoughts', allowing the model to explore multiple reasoning paths, self-evaluate states, look ahead and backtrack. NeurIPS 2023 camera-ready.

entries.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
entries.summary: Interleaves generated reasoning traces with task-specific actions so the model can both plan and query external sources. On HotpotQA and Fever, ReAct reduces the hallucination and error propagation typical of pure chain-of-thought by grounding in a Wikipedia API; on ALFWorld and WebShop it beats imitation and RL baselines by 34% and 10% absolute success rate with one or two in-context examples.

entries.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
entries.summary: Samples multiple diverse chain-of-thought reasoning paths from the same model and marginalises over them to select the most consistent final answer, rather than taking a single greedy decoding.

entries.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
entries.summary: Agents verbally reflect on task feedback and store those reflections in an episodic memory buffer to condition future trials, improving performance without updating model weights.

entries.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
entries.summary: Demonstrates that reasoning ability can be elicited by pure reinforcement learning without human-labelled reasoning trajectories. Reports emergent behaviours including self-reflection, verification of intermediate steps, and dynamic strategy adaptation, with strong results on verifiable maths, coding-competition and STEM tasks. Published in Nature 645:633-638 (2025); arXiv v2 revised 4 Jan 2026.

entries.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
entries.summary: Studies how to spend extra compute at inference time - revising responses, searching over candidate solutions, or verifying with a learned verifier - and how to allocate that compute adaptively to question difficulty.

entries.title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
entries.summary: 466 real-world questions that are conceptually simple for humans but hard for AI, requiring reasoning, multimodality handling, web browsing and general tool-use proficiency. Human respondents reach 92% while GPT-4 equipped with plugins reached 15% at publication.

entries.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
entries.summary: Analyses multi-document QA and key-value retrieval and finds a U-shaped performance curve: models perform best when the relevant information is at the beginning or end of the context and degrade significantly when it sits in the middle. Performance also falls as total context length grows, even for models advertised as long-context.

entries.title: Repository status: the classifications that override a score
entries.summary: The status vocabulary applied to repository records — active, maintenance, archived, experimental, deprecated, unverified, snapshot — how each is detected from observable GitHub facts, and the action an agent must take for each.

entries.title: Source scoring: how every repository and claim in this knowledge base is graded
entries.summary: The weighted 0-10 scoring model applied to all 414 repositories in metadata/repositories.json, the tier thresholds it produces, and the rule that makes it honest: every component is computed from observable GitHub API facts or a cited source, never from reputation, star count alone, or an invented number.

entries.title: Verification findings: what the 2026-09-15 ingestion actually discovered
entries.summary: The concrete, dated results of verifying 417 seed repositories against the GitHub API — 27 renames, 5 archived projects, 2 license-null collections, 3 nonexistent slugs, and the aggregator conflict that changed how papers are verified in this repository.

entries.title: Build vs adopt: the five questions and the third option
entries.summary: The ordered decision procedure for building, adopting or removing a capability, the cost comparison across both options, the explicit conditions for each, and the wrapper trap that turns adoption into the most expensive of both.

entries.title: System design checklist: the decisions that must be made explicitly
entries.summary: The ordered set of design decisions a system review must be able to answer — requirements as numbers, data model, consistency, failure modes, scaling, observability, security, configuration, evolution and the agent-system additions — with the omission behind each question.

entries.title: Consistency models in distributed systems: the practical ladder
entries.summary: The consistency spectrum from strong to eventual, what each level costs in latency and availability, the specific bugs each one admits, and how to choose per data type rather than per system.

entries.title: Idempotency: making retries safe
entries.summary: Why at-least-once delivery makes idempotency mandatory rather than optional, the four implementation patterns ranked by strength, the key-generation rules that determine whether they work, and the failure modes that appear only under retry storms.

entries.title: Vector search: embeddings, indexes and the retrieval decisions that matter
entries.summary: What embedding retrieval does and does not provide, the ANN index families and their parameters, chunking as the dominant quality lever, hybrid retrieval with reranking, and the evaluation that separates a working RAG system from a plausible one.

entries.title: Consistency models and transaction isolation, from the database seat
entries.summary: What each SQL isolation level actually prevents in a real engine, where write skew appears, how SERIALIZABLE differs from snapshot isolation, and the retry obligations an application takes on when it chooses the strongest level.

entries.title: Index strategy: choosing, verifying and retiring indexes
entries.summary: How to decide what to index from observed query patterns rather than guesswork, how to verify an index is used, the write-cost accounting that makes indexes expensive, and the retirement process for indexes nobody queries.

entries.title: PostgreSQL gotchas that produce silent wrong answers
entries.summary: The Postgres behaviours that differ from what developers assume — NULL semantics, MVCC and vacuum, index types that do not do what their name suggests, transaction isolation defaults, and the query patterns that defeat the planner.

entries.title: LLM-as-judge: when it is trustworthy and how to validate it
entries.summary: The known biases of LLM judges, the validation procedure that makes a judge usable as a metric, the task shapes where judging works and fails, and the calibration against human labels that turns a judge from an opinion into a measurement.

entries.title: React in practice: rendering, state and the causes of slow interfaces
entries.summary: The rendering model that makes React performance and correctness predictable — what triggers a render, where state belongs, when memoisation actually pays, the key mistakes that carry state to the wrong item, and the checklist for diagnosing a slow interface.

entries.title: Rendering strategies: choosing where and when HTML is produced
entries.summary: The CSR / SSR / SSG / ISR / streaming / RSC / islands decision — what each costs in infrastructure, latency and staleness control; the two content questions that determine the answer; and the migrations that are harder than they look.

entries.title: MCP server security: the operational checklist for enabling one
entries.summary: The pre-enablement review for an MCP server — publisher verification, source review, capability enumeration, credential scoping, sandboxing and logging — plus the runtime controls that keep a granted capability from becoming an incident.

entries.title: Backend profiling: measuring before optimising
entries.summary: The measurement-first procedure for backend performance work — what to measure, which profiler answers which question, how to read a profile without being misled by self time or off-CPU waits, and the optimisation classes ranked by typical payoff.

entries.title: Frontend performance budgets: what to measure and what to enforce
entries.summary: Concrete budgets for Core Web Vitals and payload size, the measurement methodology that makes numbers comparable, the causes of each regression class, and the CI enforcement that keeps a budget from decaying.

entries.title: Public reasoning research: what is established, contested, emerging and marketing
entries.summary: A graded survey of the public literature on LLM reasoning — chain-of-thought, self-consistency, ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, process reward models and RL-for-reasoning — with claims separated by evidence level, contested ones named as contested, and the engineering consequences of each.

entries.title: Case study: when a secondary aggregator contradicts the primary source
entries.summary: A real conflict recorded on 2026-09-15: OpenAlex returned wrong titles for two arXiv DOIs (2201.11903 and 2210.03629) while arxiv.org returned the correct ones. This document is the worked example for the conflict-resolution policy: never silently pick a winner, record both observations, resolve by source precedence, and keep the evidence trail.

entries.title: The verification workflow: eight steps from retrieval to graded claim
entries.summary: Why retrieval and verification are separate activities, the eight-step verification procedure, the precedence order for resolving disagreement between sources, and the quarantine-not-delete rule for material that cannot be graded.

entries.title: Excluded sources: what this knowledge base will never contain, and why
entries.summary: The exclusion policy for leaked system prompts, private model internals, proprietary weights and other improperly obtained material — including two high-star public repositories that are explicitly named as excluded, the reasoning, and how the policy is enforced mechanically.

entries.title: MCP threat model: what can go wrong when an agent gets tools
entries.summary: The threat model for Model Context Protocol servers and tool-using agents — prompt injection reaching a tool, confused deputy, over-broad capability grants, supply-chain risk in server packages, and the mitigations that are structural rather than advisory.

entries.title: Prompt injection defences: what actually holds and what does not
entries.summary: The layered defence model for prompt injection in agent systems — why no single control is sufficient, which mitigations are structural versus advisory, and the honest assessment of what remains unmitigated.

entries.title: Software supply chain security, including the AI-specific surface
entries.summary: Attack classes from typosquatting to dependency confusion and model poisoning, the nine controls ranked by leverage, and the agent-specific dependencies — MCP servers, skill packs, checkpoints and datasets — that classical supply-chain tooling does not cover.

entries.title: Threat modeling for agent systems
entries.summary: The four-question threat-modeling method, trust boundaries as the unit of analysis, STRIDE per element, the agent-specific threat classes STRIDE misses, and the four artifacts that prove a model happened.

entries.title: Flaky tests: diagnosis, quarantine and repair
entries.summary: The causes of non-deterministic test failure ranked by frequency, the quarantine process that keeps a failing test from destroying suite signal, and the specific repairs for each cause class.

entries.title: Test levels: what belongs where and what each level can prove
entries.summary: The unit / integration / contract / end-to-end / property / snapshot ladder, what each level can and cannot prove, the cost-benefit distribution that determines where effort goes, and the specific bugs each level is the only one able to catch.

entries.title: The AI-slop signature catalogue: what makes an interface read as machine-generated
entries.summary: The measurable symptoms that make an interface read as AI-generated, grouped by root cause, with the underlying mechanism for each. Companion reference to skills/ai-slop-detection — this file explains why the signatures exist, the skill defines how to detect and fix them.

entries.title: Visual hierarchy: the mechanisms that determine what a user sees first
entries.summary: The perceptual channels through which hierarchy is communicated — size, weight, colour, contrast, position, space, isolation and motion — how they combine and conflict, and the diagnostic for a view where nothing stands out.

entries.title: What makes a website look professional
entries.summary: The properties that read as professional — restraint, a real system, hierarchy, specific content, craft in the details — with the observable evidence for each and the reason it produces the impression it does.

entries.title: What makes an AI-built website look generic
entries.summary: The mechanism behind generic AI output — probable rather than derived choices — the six observable signature families, the tell-tale token list that makes detection mechanical, and what generic is NOT, so remediation does not produce a different cliché.
